Three months on those roads. Please tell me you had the bike checked before you rode it home.
I did not dare. I dropped it off at the workshop the next morning and asked for a quote. After that much wear and tear, a tune-up was never going to be enough.
So you had the whole thing overhauled?
Every bearing. It is more roadworthy now than the day I bought it. The problem is me. I came back to a backlog of four hundred emails and I was swamped before I had even unpacked.
That is the part nobody warns you about. I always get my brother to run my errands for the first week. Reverse culture shock is real, and it takes me a month to readjust.

Hi Marcelo, it is Kaia. You asked how bad my own homecoming was last year, so here is the honest list. I got back from Patagonia on a Tuesday, and by Wednesday I had already had the van towed, because of course it would not start after six weeks in a cold garage. Then I dropped my camera off at a shop in town, since the lens had taken a real beating, and the quote they gave me was almost the price of a new one. The wear and tear on my gear is always worse than the wear and tear on me. But the repairs were not the hard part. The office was. I had a backlog of two hundred emails and I was swamped for two solid weeks. In the end I got my brother to answer the easy ones while I dealt with the rest. So here is my advice. Do not try to readjust in a weekend. Give it a month, recharge your batteries, and have somebody else run your errands while you find your feet. Talk soon.

Welcome back to the show. Today, the part of the adventure that nobody puts in the photographs: coming home. Ask any long-distance traveler and you will hear the same thing. The trip ends, and then a second, much quieter trip begins. First there is the gear. Something always needs fixing, so you drop it off, you ask for a quote, and you discover that three months of wear and tear costs more than three months of flights. Then there is the house. You get the mail sorted, you have the water heater looked at, you get somebody to help you dig out from the backlog on your desk. And then there is you. Reverse culture shock is the strange, unglamorous truth of travel. The hardest border to cross is the one back into your own kitchen. So be patient with yourself. Give it a month. Recharge your batteries, get the small things done, and do not judge a journey by how quickly you readjust afterwards. The road changed you. Let home catch up.

First, the writer rides the last two hundred kilometers and reaches his own street with the bike barely holding together. Then, the next morning, he drops the bike off at the workshop and asks for a quote. After that, the mechanic tells him a tune-up is not enough, so he has the whole thing overhauled. Next, at home, he is swamped by a backlog of four hundred emails, so he gets the mail sorted and gets his sister to drive him around. Finally, he has his best photographs printed, hangs them on the wall, and gives himself a month to readjust.
